abstract: Diagnosis of stroke in young and otherwise healthy individuals is rare, but early detection and treatment are crucial to patient outcomes. There may be unusual factors that lead to a presentation of stroke as seen in this case.

title: From single pathways to holistic networks: unraveling the multimechanistic actions of acupuncture in depression.
abstract: Depression is a globally prevalent mental disorder; however, current pharmacological treatments are limited by a delayed onset of action and significant adverse effects. As a safe and effective non-pharmacological therapy, acupuncture demonstrates unique advantages in treating mild to moderate depression. Its antidepressant mechanisms are multifaceted. Primarily, acupuncture mitigates neuroinflammation by inhibiting classical signaling pathways (e.g., nuclear factor kappa B/NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3), modulating microglial polarization, and restoring cytokine homeostasis. Furthermore, it enhances neuroplasticity by upregulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression, improving synaptic plasticity, and promoting adult neurogenesis. At the cellular level, acupuncture exerts neuroprotective effects by suppressing apoptotic cascades associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and endoplasmic reticulum stress, regulating autophagic balance, and restoring neuronal excitability. Systemically, it ameliorates metabolic dysregulation by optimizing cerebral energy metabolism, modulating gut microbiota composition, and reinforcing intestinal barrier integrity. Additionally, acupuncture effectively alleviates comorbid pain by modulating peripheral nociceptive signaling and central pain-emotion feedback loops. These synergistic effects across multiple systems and targets may together ameliorate the pathophysiological alterations associated with depression. Despite these advances, current research faces challenges, including the translational gap between animal models and clinical pathology, as well as an insufficient investigation of multi-mechanism interactions. Future efforts should focus on developing clinically relevant models, integrating multi-omics technologies, conducting high-quality clinical trials, and exploring biomarker-guided personalized treatments to advance the scientific and standardized application of acupuncture for depression.

title: A novel technique for visualizing in vivo dynamic neuronal changes during Drosophila development.
abstract: A major limitation in neurobiology is the inability to precisely track in vivo neuronal morphology over time. Tandem dimer Eos (TdEOS), a fluorescent photoconvertible protein under UV light, enables visualization and quantification of morphological changes between timepoints in a single animal. We optimized this using the Drosophila Moonwalker Descending Neuron (MDN), which undergoes morphological changes and is genetically accessible. By expressing TdEOS in MDNs, we demonstrated successful in vivo photoconversion, confocal imaging, and quantification of dendrite morphology changes between two timepoints in the same animal. Ultimately, TdEOS provides a targeted, accessible tool for tracing complex neuronal morphology overtime in vivo .

title: Reprogramming the gut-brain axis in neurodegeneration: comparative microbiome, metabolite, immunometabolic, polyphenol, probiotic, and epigenetic mechanisms in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.
abstract: The gut-brain axis has emerged as a central mechanistic framework linking dietary bioactives, microbial ecology, and neurodegenerative disease progression. Similar microbiome-related mechanisms have also been implicated in colorectal cancer, suggesting potential shared links between microbial dysbiosis, inflammation, and disease progression. This study synthesizes preclinical evidence examining how polyphenols, polyphenol-derived compounds, and advanced delivery systems, including nanoparticles and synbiotics, modulate Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) through microbiome-dependent mechanisms. Evidence from transgenic mice, toxin-induced rodent models, and Drosophila systems was compared across microbiome alterations, microbial metabolites, signaling pathways, epigenetic regulation, and functional outcomes. Across AD and PD models, dietary bioactives consistently promoted restoration of gut microbial homeostasis, characterized by enrichment of beneficial taxa and reduction of dysbiosis-associated microorganisms. These changes were accompanied by alterations in microbial metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan-derived metabolites, and lipid-associated signaling molecules. These metabolites provide functional links between microbial ecology and CNS physiology and may regulate epigenetic processes, including histone acetylation, DNA methylation, chromatin remodeling, and non-coding RNA activity. Despite substantial upstream convergence, downstream effects showed disease-specific patterns. In AD models, microbiome modulation predominantly influenced metabolic, amyloidogenic, and neurotrophic pathways, including AKT/GSK3β, NRF2, NF-κB, and BDNF-associated signaling, contributing to reduced amyloid-β deposition, attenuated tau pathology, and improved cognitive outcomes. In PD models, greater emphasis was placed on inflammatory, oxidative, and mitochondrial pathways involving SIRT1/NRF2, TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB, inflammasome signaling, and neuronal survival mechanisms, resulting in reduced neuroinflammation and preservation of dopaminergic neurons and motor function. Epigenetic regulation represents an additional convergence layer through which microbial metabolites and polyphenols may influence inflammatory, metabolic, mitochondrial, and neuronal gene programs in both disorders. Nanoparticle-based delivery systems enhanced bioavailability, tissue targeting, and microbiome-related effects, whereas synbiotic strategies reinforced microbial and metabolic homeostasis. Collectively, these findings support a microbiome-metabolite-epigenome-brain framework in which dietary bioactives modulate neurodegeneration through interconnected microbial, metabolic, immune, redox, mitochondrial, and epigenetic pathways. This framework provides a mechanistic basis for developing disease-tailored and precision-oriented gut-brain interventions for AD and PD.

title: Detection of Supporting-Cell-Associated Gene Transcripts in Adult Human Cochlear Tissue from Cadaveric Temporal Bones.
abstract: The adult human cochlea is difficult to study because viable inner-ear tissue is rarely available and postmortem samples are technically challenging to process. Supporting cells are essential for cochlear architecture, ionic and osmotic balance, synaptic stability, stress responses, and potential regenerative signaling. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the feasibility of detecting transcripts associated with cochlear supporting-cell biology in adult human cadaveric cochlear tissue. Bilateral temporal bones were obtained from six adult cadaveric donors within 24 hours of death, yielding 12 temporal bones. One temporal bone from each donor was processed for cochlear microdissection and RNA isolation. RNA suitable for downstream analysis was recovered from five of the six processed cochlear specimens. Total RNA was treated with DNase I, converted to cDNA, and analyzed by endpoint RT-PCR for AQP4, GLAST (SLC1A3/EAAT1), TAK1 (MAP3K7), and SOX21. All four transcripts were detected in each of the five analyzable cochlear specimens (5/5 for AQP4, 5/5 for GLAST (SLC1A3/EAAT1), 5/5 for TAK1 (MAP3K7), and 5/5 for SOX21). These findings provide preliminary molecular evidence that AQP4, GLAST (SLC1A3/EAAT1), TAK1 (MAP3K7), and SOX21 transcripts, representing biological processes related to water and osmotic homeostasis, glutamate handling, stress-response signaling, and developmental/progenitor-associated transcriptional regulation, are detectable in adult human cadaveric cochlear tissue. Because the analysis was performed on bulk cochlear tissue rather than purified supporting cells, the detected transcripts should be interpreted as supporting-cell-associated rather than supporting-cell-specific. The study demonstrates the feasibility of RNA-based transcript detection from postmortem adult human cochlear tissue using endpoint RT-PCR and provides a foundation for future validation using quantitative RT-PCR, RNA scope, immunostaining, single-cell or single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics.

title: Curcumin in the Treatment of Various Diseases: Mechanism of Action, Bioavailability, Therapeutic Effects, and Current Clinical Trials.
abstract: Curcumin is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound with anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiapoptotic, and anticancer properties. Numerous studies have demonstrated that curcumin can regulate multiple molecular targets, including signaling pathways such as Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88)/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), Janus kinase (JAK)/signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT), PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin, Parkin, phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)/antioxidant response element (ARE). Notably, curcumin exhibits therapeutic potential in a variety of diseases, including neurological disorders, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, inflammatory diseases, and autoimmune diseases. Its mechanisms of action are associated with the suppression of inflammation, regulation of mitochondrial dysfunction, inhibition of apoptosis, attenuation of oxidative stress, and enhancement of neuroplasticity. However, the extremely low oral bioavailability of curcumin limits its application in disease therapy. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in curcumin research, including its pharmacological properties, molecular mechanisms of action, and nanodelivery systems, such as nanoparticles, liposomes, nanoemulsions, polymeric micelles, and exosomes, which have been developed to enhance curcumin bioavailability. Furthermore, this review provides an in-depth overview of the therapeutic benefits of curcumin in neurological disorders, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, inflammatory diseases, and autoimmune diseases. It focuses on evidence from in vitro studies, in vivo experiments, and potential clinical applications, while also discusses the therapeutic potential, current challenges, and future perspectives of curcumin in disease management.

title: The potential pathological role of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in pediatric tic disorders and its therapeutic implications.
abstract: Tic disorders (TDs) are common neurodevelopmental disorders in children and adolescents, with pathophysiology involving abnormalities in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuits, neurotransmitter imbalance, and neuroimmune dysregulation. In recent years, the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome has attracted increasing attention because of its role in linking cellular stress, innate immunity, and inflammatory responses. Current human TD/Tourette syndrome (TS) studies primarily support striatal neuroimmune abnormalities and microglial inflammatory changes, whereas more direct evidence for NLRP3-, caspase-1-, and gasdermin D (GSDMD)-related alterations is derived mainly from animal models. Mechanistic evidence that NLRP3-related inflammation can influence synaptic function and neural circuits largely comes from non-TD experimental models. This review summarizes the activation mechanisms and biological effects of the NLRP3 inflammasome, with particular emphasis on its potential links to striatal neuroinflammation, pyroptosis-related effects, neurotransmitter regulation, and CSTC network abnormalities. We also discuss the pharmacological feasibility and evidentiary limitations of upstream modulation, direct NLRP3 inhibition, and blockade of downstream inflammatory effectors. At present, disease-specific causal validation of NLRP3 and direct evidence for NLRP3-targeted interventions in pediatric TDs remain lacking. Future studies integrating disease-specific mechanistic validation, biomarker development, and patient stratification are needed to clarify the pathological relevance and potential translational significance of NLRP3 in pediatric TDs.

title: Blood TRPC6 mRNA as a biomarker for Alzheimer's disease: a nationwide, multicenter study in China.
abstract: Accessible blood-based biomarkers remain needed for Alzheimer's disease (AD) screening and diagnosis. We investigated whether blood transient receptor potential canonical 6 (TRPC6) could serve as a potential biomarker for AD. We enrolled 1254 individuals, including 366 patients with AD, 735 cognitively unimpaired (CU) individuals, and 153 individuals with non-AD neurological disorders. All patients with AD were confirmed to be amyloid beta positive (Aβ+) by Aβ positron emission tomography (PET). Blood TRPC6 messenger RNA (mRNA) levels were measured in all participants. In a subset, Aβ PET imaging and plasma biomarker assessments were performed. Blood TRPC6 mRNA levels differed significantly among the CU, AD, and non-AD groups, with the lowest levels observed in patients with AD. TRPC6 mRNA levels were associated with regional Aβ deposition and showed diagnostic performance comparable to several established plasma biomarkers, although slightly inferior to phosphorylated tau 217. Blood TRPC6 mRNA is markedly reduced in AD and may represent an accessible and clinically relevant blood biomarker for AD.

title: Corrigendum to "How do network structures of depressive symptoms differ between asian patients with bipolar depression and those with unipolar depression?" [Asian J. Psychiatry 122 (2026) 105062].
Creative cognition in frontotemporal dementia and brain health.
abstract: Creative cognition is central to human thought and is affected by brain disease. Recent findings by Altmayer and colleagues link creative impairment in frontotemporal dementia to rostral prefrontal functional differentiation. These findings motivate a framework for investigating network coordination, circuit physiology, experience-dependent plasticity, and bodily and social regulation in creativity and health.

title: Characterising the plasma metabolome following high intensity interval exercise in continuous and intermittent hypoxia in overweight individuals.
abstract: The aim of this work was to examine changes in the plasma metabolome in response to high-intensity interval exercise (HIIE) performed under three distinct hypoxia protocols. On separate days, 18 inactive individuals with overweight completed a HIIE protocol in randomised conditions: normoxia (NEx-NRec), normobaric hypoxia (inspired O2 fraction ∼0.14) during both the work and recovery (HEx-HRec), normobaric hypoxia during recovery only (NEx-HRec) and normobaric hypoxia during work only (HEx-NRec). Venous blood samples were collected before and after each HIIE for metabolite analyses by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry and 1H-nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Mean power output, averaged across the six work bouts, was lower in HEx-HRec compared to NEx-NRec, NEx-HRec and HEx-NRec (all P ≤ 0.009), with no differences (all P ≥ 0.11) between the other conditions. Arterial oxygen saturation was lower in HEx-HRec compared to other conditions (all P 0.37). The lactate to pyruvate ratio increased in all conditions, but did not differ between them. Free-fatty acid (FFA) classes (saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated FFAs) showed consistent increases (all P < 0.001), while monounsaturated and saturated triacylglycerol (TAG) classes significantly decreased following HIIE (both P < 0.04). There were no condition × time interaction effects for any metabolites. HIIE significantly altered the concentration of glycolytic and TCA cycle intermediates, whilst concomitantly increasing FFA and decreasing TAG concentrations. Although hypoxia applied either continuously throughout HIIE or intermittently (work or recovery) during HIIE altered exercise performance and oxygen saturation, it had limited additional effect on metabolite concentrations.

title: Effects of maternal exposure to 2,6-dichloro-1,4-benzoquinone during pregnancy and lactation on the gut microbiota and neurodevelopment in offspring rats.
abstract: 2,6-dichloro-1,4-benzoquinone (DCBQ), as an emerging drinking water disinfection byproduct, has been widely detected in drinking water and pose potential risks. However, there are relatively few reports on their potential neurodevelopmental toxicity, especially the lack of in vivo studies as the most direct evidence. A rat model was established for the entire gestation and lactation period to study the neurodevelopmental toxicity of DCBQ in offspring rats, through evaluating gut microbiota, neurotransmitters and neurobehaviors. Maternal rats were administered with DCBQ at 0.5, 5, and 50 mg/kg body weight via gavage throughout gestation and lactation. Our results showed that maternal DCBQ exposure induced prolonged neural reflex behavior, decreased motor activity, and increased anxiety-like behavior in offspring rats. And the levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factors and neurotransmitters, especially glutamate and dopamine, in serum and hippocampus were significantly decreased in offspring rats after maternal DCBQ exposure. Maternal DCBQ exposure induced imbalance of intestinal microbiota in a gender-specific way. In addition, maternal DCBQ exposure induced significant changes of 123 metabolites, affecting multiple metabolic pathways, such as mTOR pathway. In particular, the altered gut microbiota showed strong associations with altered metabolites, neurotransmitters and neurobehaviors after maternal DCBQ exposure. Our findings suggest that maternal DCBQ exposure may impair neurodevelopment and disrupt gut microbiota and fecal metabolite profiles of offspring rats, indicating a potential gut microbiota-metabolome-neurochemical link. Our study highlights the importance of evaluating the neurodevelopmental toxicity of disinfection byproducts in future.

title: Mangiferin Buffers Depressive-Like Behaviors by Modulating Astrocytic DHHC2 in the Hippocampus.
abstract: Several lines of evidence indicate that mangiferin (MGF) ameliorates chronic stress-induced anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors, yet its precise role and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that MGF effectively alleviates anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors in mice exposed to chronic stress, accompanied by reduced synaptic loss and ameliorated hippocampal neurogenesis deficits. Notably, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) expression is preferentially altered in hippocampal astrocytes but not in neurons or microglia after chronic stress and MGF treatment, and knockdown of astrocytic Nrf2 abrogates the antidepressant effect of MGF. Further mechanistic studies showed that MGF reverses reactive astrogliosis by regulating astrocytic DHHC2-Nrf2 signaling, including Nrf2 palmitoylation and its nuclear translocation, thereby protecting Nrf2 from Keap1-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation and sustaining its transcriptional activity in reactive astrocytes. These findings demonstrate that MGF alleviates chronic stress-induced anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors by engaging the astrocytic DHHC2-Nrf2 signaling, suppressing reactive astrogliosis and reversing hippocampal synaptic and neurogenic deficits, which provides novel insights into the therapeutic potential of MGF for chronic stress-related mood disorders.

title: Effectiveness of Upfront Radiotherapy in Central Nervous System Germ Cell Tumors.
abstract: Radiotherapy (RT) is essential for curing central nervous system germ cell tumors (CNS-GCTs) except for pure mature teratoma (MT), but the optimal target volume, dose, and timing remain controversial. This study evaluated the benefit of upfront RT in CNS-GCTs. We reviewed CNS-GCT patients under 30-year-old treated from 2015 to 2023. Patients with pure germinomas (PG) received whole-ventricular irradiation (WVI) with tumor bed (TB) boost. Patients with malignant non-germinomatous germ cell tumor (MNGGCT) received WVI or whole-brain irradiation (WBI) with TB boost, with or without craniospinal irradiation (CSI), before or after platinum-etoposide-based chemotherapy (CTX). Serum alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin levels guided diagnosis when histopathology was unavailable. Patients with MT were treated surgically. The primary endpoint was 5-year event-free survival (EFS); secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), neurocognitive outcomes, and endocrinopathy rates. Twenty-nine patients were analyzed: 13 PGs, 7 MNGGCTs with upfront RT, 7 MNGGCTs with upfront CTX, and 2 MTs. The median follow-up of these tumors was 6.0, 6.6, 3.7, and 10.3 years, respectively. PGs receiving upfront RT achieved 5-year EFS and OS of 100% and 100%, respectively. For MNGGCTs receiving upfront RT, 5-year EFS and OS was 85.7% and 85.7%, respectively; 1 patient died from post-treatment disease progression. MNGGCTs treated with upfront CTX had 5-year EFS and OS of 41.7% and 60.0%, respectively; 2 patients relapsed (1 died), and 1 died from treatment-related complications. Both MTs remained event-free over 6 years following surgery alone or with Gamma Knife radiosurgery. Upfront RT provided excellent outcomes in PGs and may eliminate the need for CTX in those achieving complete response.

title: Optimizing cognitive and behavioural recovery after stroke: clinical integration of dietary supplements with a focus on ω-3 fatty acids.
abstract: Stroke remains a leading cause of long-term disability worldwide, with many survivors experiencing persistent cognitive and behavioural impairments despite advancements in acute management. Post-stroke neurorecovery is often incomplete, contributing to dementia, depression, and reduced quality of life, particularly in low- and middle-income settings where access to advanced rehabilitation and therapeutics is limited. This highlights an urgent need for accessible, adjunctive strategies that can enhance functional recovery. Emerging preclinical evidence indicates that dietary supplements can modulate key biological processes underlying neurorecovery, including neuroplasticity, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and synaptic remodeling. In this narrative review, we examine the role of major classes of nutraceuticals such as omega-3 fatty acids, vitamins, minerals, polyphenols, and amino acids in supporting cognitive and behavioural recovery after stroke with particular emphasis on omega-3 fatty acids, given their central role in neuronal membrane integrity, lipid-mediated signaling, and resolution of inflammation. We integrate mechanistic insights with preclinical and clinical data explicitly highlighting that theoretical models and basic research demonstrate significant promise, while current clinical evidence remains heterogeneous and frequently inconclusive. We discuss how dietary supplementation might be strategically incorporated alongside conventional rehabilitation paradigms including physiotherapycognitive training, and pharmacotherapy. We further highlight emerging concepts such as the gut-brain axis, precision nutrition, and biomarker-guided interventions, which are shaping the future of personalized neurorehabilitation. Ultimately, while dietary supplements offer a promising, cost-effective and accessible adjunctive approach. their current clinical utility is constrained by mixed translational efficacy. Overcoming these limitations will require rigorous patient selection, optimized timing, and shift towards evidence-based personalized, multimodal strategies. This will be essential to fully harness their therapeutic potential in improving cognitive and behavioural outcomes in stroke recovery.

title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic insights into neural substrates of Behavioural dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: The transition from bulk-tissue profiling to single-cell and spatially resolved transcriptomics has reshaped our understanding of Alzheimer's disease (AD) from a passive proteinopathy to a coordinated multicellular process spanning the neurovascular unit. However, translating these molecular catalogues into disease-modifying therapies requires a framework that links cellular transitions to neural circuit dysfunction and behavioural abnormalities. This review synthesizes the multicellular landscape of AD, tracing how cell-state-specific remodelling drives network collapse and cognitive decline. Neuronally, selective vulnerability targets projection networks and subclass-specific inhibitory interneurons. Their transcriptional silencing compromises projection pathways, including the entorhinal-hippocampal perforant path, disrupts cortical microcircuits, and underlies episodic memory impairment, hyperexcitability, and executive control failure. This neuronal degeneration is dynamically coupled to reactive glial and vascular remodelling across distinct spatial niches. We examine the non-linear transition of homeostatic astrocytes and microglia into specialized, plaque-associated reactive sub-states, as well as paracrine signalling decay at the neurovascular interface. Compromised capillary tight junctions and the shedding of pericytic survival receptors are proposed to promote blood-brain barrier disintegrity, triggering a feed-forward neuroinflammatory cascade of complement-mediated synaptic pruning. Crucially, we establish a three-tiered hierarchy of evidence, rigorously distinguishing cross-sectional, associative human postmortem findings from inferred functional trajectories in human cellular platforms, and causal, perturbation-based validations in transgenic rodent models. We review how contemporary multi-scale integration-combining single-nucleus transcriptomics with functional electrophysiological platforms and biophysical connectomic modelling-bridges the gap between terminal postmortem signatures and living brain dynamics. Finally, we outline a coordinated translational roadmap illustrating how spatially resolved cell-state networks can guide the development of fluid and imaging biomarkers, support biologically informed patient stratification, enrich clinical trials, and accelerate the development of circuit-restoring precision therapies, thereby providing a mechanistic framework that links cell-state transitions to neural circuit dysfunction, behavioural impairment, and precision medicine in Alzheimer's disease.

title: The Separation-Distress Network as a Transdiagnostic Mechanism Linking Relational Adversity, Social Pain, and Psychopathology.
abstract: Relational trauma is a major contributor to the development of mental health disorders. This association likely reflects the social nature of humans and other mammals, whose survival depends on maintaining stable social bonds. When these bonds are threatened or disrupted, individuals experience social pain, a distress response mediated by the mammalian separation-distress network. During early development, this network is sensitive to maintaining proximity with caregivers, as independent survival is not yet possible. Converging evidence from ethology, psychodynamic and attachment theory, and social and affective neuroscience supports the function of this network. Because mammalian brains are inherently tuned to form social bonds, adverse relational experiences can disrupt socioemotional development and increase vulnerability to psychopathology. Neural substrates of separation distress include the anterior cingulate cortex, ventral septum, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, dorsal preoptic area, dorsomedial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray, with endogenous opioids and glucocorticoids serving as key neurochemical modulators in the separation-distress response. Separation distress and adverse relational experiences also alter physiological systems implicated in psychopathology, including the HPA axis, autonomic nervous system activity, inflammation, and brain structure and connectivity. This paper argues that relational trauma and social pain are mediated by an evolutionarily conserved subcortical separation-distress network shared across predominantly mammalian species. Dysregulation of this network may represent one common mechanism underlying depression, social anxiety, suicidality, substance use disorders, borderline personality disorder, and other psychiatric conditions. Understanding the processes linking adverse relational experiences, separation-distress activation, and social pain may provide insights into the etiology and treatment of diverse disorders.

title: Studying the pharmacological interaction of temozolomide chemotherapy with different antidepressant treatments in a rat glioblastoma model.
abstract: The present study evaluated the pharmacological interaction of temozolomide (TMZ) chemotherapy with 3 potential antidepressant treatments (cannabidiol, CBD; fluoxetine, FLX; metformin, MET) in a rat glioblastoma model with the objective of finding drug combinations to better treat the depressive symptoms observed in glioblastoma patients. Methods Adult male Fisher 344 rats were inoculated with syngeneic RG2 cells into the right striatum. Then, rats received the antitumoral drug (TMZ, 25 mg/kg) vs. its vehicle (C-group), and 3 h later, treated with CBD (30 mg/kg), FLX (10 mg/kg), MET (100 mg/kg) or vehicle (Veh-group) for 5 days. The forced-swim test was used to score antidepressant-like responses. Markers of treatment response were evaluated in brain samples (hippocampal neurogenesis) of the non-tumor-infiltrated hemisphere and in blood plasma (corticosterone and immune system cells). Results The main results showed that TMZ alone and/or in combination with different types of potential antidepressants (CBD, FLX, MET) did not alter behavioral performance assessed in the forced-swim test. The absence of behavioral effects, however, is not attributed to a lack of pharmacological effects of the specific drugs. TMZ treatment decreased body weight gain, reduced the number of hippocampal neural progenitors and diminished immune plasma markers, while CBD and FLX decreased plasma corticosterone. Conclusion In conjunction, our results did not support the hypothesis of a beneficial use of antidepressants as a combinational therapy with TMZ to attenuate the most associated comorbidity of glioblastoma, depression, at least in male rats with this specific model of experimentally induced glioblastoma.

title: Information, Mass, Energy Principles: A biophysical and ecological framework for understanding the brain.
abstract: The brain is a highly complex biological system whose structure, function, and evolution are constrained by material resources and energy availability, as any other natural system. Here, we extend the ecological Information-Mass-Energy (IME) framework (Peñuelas, 2024) to neuroscience. In contrast to purely computational models, we propose that the brain is an information-organizing system constrained by mass availability, energetic expenditure, and thermodynamic efficiency. Through comparative analyses across mammalian species, we identify a superlinear scaling relationship between white and grey matter volumes, alongside a positive association between white matter volume and inhibitory-control performance. This suggests that neural organization contribute to cognitive capacities beyond brain size alone. Integrating these findings with metabolic scaling principles, we propose that brain evolution involves trade-offs between increasing informational complexity and the material and energetic costs required to sustain it. Within this framework, we formulate testable hypotheses concerning how informational organization may scale with neural material and energetic expenditure. Furthermore, we introduce a quantitative disturbance-recovery model that incorporates carrying capacity, recovery rate, and disturbance magnitude and duration, generating testable predictions for neurological conditions such as stroke and neurodegeneration. By combining empirical scaling relationships with a mathematical framework for neural organization, energetic constraints, and resilience, the IME framework offers a novel biophysical and ecological perspective on brain evolution and function. This framework also provides a foundation for investigating energetically sustainable information processing in biological and artificial systems.

title: Astragalus membranaceus-derived exosomes deliver calycosin to orchestrate the Nrf2/SLC7A11/GPX4 axis against ferroptosis in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Astragalus membranaceus (Fisch.) Bunge (Fabaceae) is documented in Shennong's Classic of Materia Medica to treat Qi deficiency-induced cerebral blood stasis and limb tremor resembling Parkinson's disease (PD). Its primary bioactive component, calycosin (CA), exerts anti-ferroptosis effects; however, its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is severely limited. Herbal-derived exosomes isolated from Astragalus membranaceus act as homologous natural nanocarriers to overcome this limitation; however, the anti-PD efficacy and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)-dependent ferroptosis regulatory mechanism of Astragalus membranaceus-derived exosomes (AS-Exos) loaded with CA (AS-Exos-CA) remain unelucidated. To construct AS-Exos-CA, verify both its BBB-crossing capacity and neuroprotective effect on dopaminergic neurons, and investigate whether its anti-ferroptosis protection relies on the Nrf2/SLC7A11/GPX4 axis, to provide modern pharmacological evidence for the ethnopharmacological application of Astragalus membranaceus against PD. AS-Exos were isolated by ultracentrifugation and characterized using NTA and TEM. HPLC was employed to screen the optimal CA-loading ratio for preparing AS-Exos-CA and measure its encapsulation efficiency. PKH26 and DiR fluorescence labeling were used to assess cellular uptake and BBB penetration of AS-Exos-CA in PC12 cells and 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced mice, respectively. Motor function, dopaminergic neuron survival, ferroptosis-related oxidative stress, iron metabolism and mitochondrial ultrastructure were assessed to evaluate the therapeutic effects of AS-Exos-CA in MPTP-induced PD mice. 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium ion (MPP+)-injured PC12 cells combined with the Nrf2-specific inhibitor ML385 were used to verify the Nrf2-dependent mechanism mediating AS-Exos-CA-derived protection. AS-Exos-CA displayed typical vesicle morphology, was efficiently taken up by PC12 cells, and significantly accumulated in mouse brain 12 h after intravenous injection. Compared with free CA and AS-Exos, AS-Exos-CA more effectively ameliorated motor deficits, rescued dopaminergic neurons, mitigated mitochondrial injury and iron deposition, restored glutathione (GSH), and lowered malondialdehyde (MDA) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. AS-Exos-CA facilitated Nrf2 nuclear translocation and up-regulated the downstream expression of SLC7A11 and GPX4. ML385 abolished its in vitro anti-ferroptotic actions, verifying the essential role of Nrf2 signaling. AS-Exos serve as homologous herbal nanocarriers, enhancing CA penetration across the BBB for brain delivery. AS-Exos-CA exerts robust neuroprotection against PD largely by inhibiting neuronal ferroptosis via the Nrf2/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway. This herbal exosome-based nanoformulation overcomes the biocompatibility limitations of synthetic nanomaterials and represents a promising disease-modifying strategy for PD, thereby advancing the modern investigation of Qi-tonifying herbal medicines in degenerative central nervous system (CNS) disorders.

title: Fixed Dose Inferior Oblique Recession Has Self-Adjusting Effect.
abstract: This study aimed to determine the effect of a uniform dose of unilateral inferior oblique muscle (IO) recession on incomitant hypertropia. Retrospective consecutive case series. Thirty-three patients with incomitant hypertropia who underwent identical unilateral IO recession between June 2015 and June 2025. Patients underwent unilateral IO recession by a single surgeon who reinserted the IO 4 mm posterior and 3 mm temporal to the temporal pole of the inferior rectus insertion. Hypertropia was measured in distant central and secondary gazes, and centrally at near. Surgical effects were evaluated by linear regression. Postoperative hypertropia, incomitance, retreatment, and relationship of initial deviation to surgical effect. Mean patient age was 40±27 (standard deviation) years, and follow-up averaged 448±562 days. Twenty patients had superior oblique palsy. Mean hypertropia in central gaze decreased after IO recession from 8.8±7.9Δ to 1.2±2.9Δ, and in contralateral gaze from 17.0±9.6Δ to 2.1±3.6Δ. Mean preoperative horizontal incomitance decreased after IO recession from 13.7±8.4Δ to 2.4±4.1Δ. Mean vertical incomitance decreased from 6.8Δ to 2.0±4.4Δ. Surgical effect was proportionately greater with greater preoperative hypertropia, resulting on average in nearly ideal correction of all hypertropia at distance in central, ipsilateral, contralateral, as well as in near gazes. This effect generally eliminated incomitance. Three (9%) patients required additional strabismus treatment. Fixed-dose IO recession corrects a wide range of incomitant hypertropia in a self-grading manner, achieving excellent effect for a wide range of hypertropia and incomitance.

title: Stroboscopic light stimulation in adults reporting depressive symptoms: Safety, tolerability, feasibility, and active-comparator development in a staged early-phase study.
abstract: Stroboscopic light stimulation (SLS) is a candidate non-pharmacological intervention that induces transient visual and affective experiences, with potential application in depression. Before efficacy testing, clinical development requires safety, tolerability, and feasibility data. We report a staged, single-site programme in adults reporting depressive symptoms. Study 1 tested 11 SLS parameter sets for safety and tolerability. Study 2 assessed whether an active comparator reduced subjective visual effects while preserving session context. Study 3 randomised 84 participants to four weekly supervised 31-minute sessions of strobe-emphasis or wash-emphasis SLS. In Study 1, 31 participants were analysed; no severe adverse reactions occurred, mean discomfort was low (0.49/10), and the highest session-level upper 80% confidence limit was 1.13/10, well below the prespecified threshold. Study 2 supported within-participant experiential separation between the two SLS configurations in healthy adults. In Study 3, endpoint data were available for 70/84 randomised participants (83.3%): 39/42 assigned to strobe-emphasis and 31/42 assigned to wash-emphasis. Discomfort remained low, with no serious SLS-attributable adverse events. Both configurations produced visual phenomenology in the Study 3 target sample, and the phenomenological separation observed during Study 2 was not reproduced between groups in Study 3. The comparison estimates differences between two active SLS configurations, rather than SLS versus no stimulation. Exploratory depressive-symptom estimates were imprecise, limited by differential endpoint availability, and should inform endpoint selection and subsequent trial design rather than efficacy. Overall, the programme supports further controlled evaluation of supervised SLS while identifying experiential separation, retention, masking, and endpoint selection as priorities for the next trial.

title: "Advancing Behavioral Neuroscience: New Tools and Techniques for Measuring Behavior".
abstract: Bridging neural activity and behavior remains a central challenge in neuroscience. Advances in quantitative behavioral measurement, automated tracking, machine learning, and multimodal recording now make it possible to characterize actions at spatial and temporal scales that were previously difficult to access. However, increased measurement capacity does not necessarily translate into better biological inference. New tools must be evaluated for measurement validity, reproducibility, robustness across experimental conditions, interpretability, and accessibility to other laboratories. This Special Issue of the Journal of Neuroscience Methods brings together methodological developments and applications spanning animal and human research, from temporal pattern analysis and automated behavioral phenotyping to integrated electrophysiological and neuroimaging approaches. Together, these contributions illustrate how transparent workflows, rigorous benchmarking, and integration of behavior with neural measurements can improve the study of brain-behavior relationships while exposing the limitations that still constrain generalization and mechanistic interpretation.

title: Effects of Physical Activity and Sports Type on Executive Functions and Socioemotional Skills of Children and Adolescents With Autism Spectrum Disorder: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence on the effects of physical activity and sports on executive functions and socioemotional skills in autistic youth, according to the intervention cognitive-motor engagement. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, 32 studies were analyzed using random-effects models with Hedges' g. Subgroup analyses and meta-regressions examined the effects of study design, intervention type, and dose. Physical activity and sports interventions showed beneficial effects on inhibitory control, communication, socialization, stereotyped behaviors, and social impairment. Physically conditioning, cognitively engaging, and combined interventions all showed positive effects, with larger effects generally observed for combined interventions. Team sports were particularly promising, showing significant effects for inhibition and socioemotional outcomes. Meta-regressions suggested domain-specific dose associations, with total intervention minutes predicting inhibition gains and total intervention weeks predicting effects on cognitive flexibility. Successful interventions often featured close supervision, progressive task difficulty, and structured social interaction. Findings support physical activity and sports as a promising, mechanism-informed approach for autistic youth.

title: Neuropeptide Systems in Substance use Disorders: Therapeutic evidence and molecular mechanisms.
abstract: Substance use disorders remain a major global health challenge, with limited pharmacological options and no approved medications for several addictive substances. Peptide-based therapeutics have emerged as promising candidates because they regulate neural circuits involved in reward, motivation, stress, and energy homeostasis. This narrative review summarizes current evidence for therapeutic peptides in substance use disorders, examines their molecular mechanisms, evaluates advances in peptide engineering and delivery technologies, and discusses future translational and precision-medicine strategies. A structured narrative review was conducted according to the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Google Scholar, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched (January 2000-July 2026) using controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to therapeutic peptides, receptors, delivery systems, and substance use disorders. Fifteen peptide and neuropeptide systems were identified. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists currently show the strongest clinical evidence, particularly for alcohol use disorder, while findings for nicotine, cocaine, and opioid use disorders remain limited. Oxytocin, orexin receptor antagonists, ghrelin, and dynorphin-related therapies demonstrate encouraging early findings. In contrast, corticotropin-releasing factor type-1 and neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists show target engagement without consistent clinical benefit. Several systems, including neuropeptide Y, galanin, pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide, cocaine- and amphetamine-regulated transcript, melanocortins, and enkephalins, remain largely preclinical. Advances in peptide engineering, nanotechnology, blood-brain barrier delivery, intranasal administration, and long-acting formulations may overcome pharmacokinetic limitations. Peptide therapeutics represent a rapidly evolving strategy for addiction treatment. Future progress will depend on integrating peptide engineering, targeted delivery platforms, biomarker-guided patient selection, and well-designed clinical trials to expand effective.

title: Retraction notice to "Analysis of psychopathological comorbidity behind the common symptoms and signs of endometriosis" [Eur. J. Obstetr. Gynecol. Rep. Biol. 194 (2015) 30-33].
journal: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology

title: Corrigendum to "Neuroprotective effects of lixisenatide and liraglutide in the MPTP mouse model of Parkinson's disease" [Neuroscience 303 (2015) 42-50].
Combined exposure of copper and iron induces nerve damage in Caenorhabditis elegans through ROS-induced autophagy/mitophagy.
abstract: Copper (Cu) and iron (Fe) are essential trace elements that become biotoxic in excess. Their widespread coexistence in the environment poses a significant risk of co-exposure to human populations. This study aimed to elucidate the combined toxic effects and underlying mechanisms of Cu and Fe using Caenorhabditis elegans as a model organism. Our results demonstrated that combined exposure to Cu and Fe synergistically inhibited motor behaviors, including head thrashes and body bends, to a greater extent than individual metal exposures. Furthermore, this co-exposure exacerbated the degeneration of both dopaminergic (DAergic) and GABAergic neurons, revealing a potent synergistic neurotoxic effect. Mechanistic investigations indicated that the combined exposure group exhibited a significant increase in both cellular and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS), pointing to severe oxidative stress as a primary driver of toxicity. This oxidative stress led to profound mitochondrial damage, characterized by a reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and ultrastructural defects, such as rupture and cristae loss, as observed via transmission electron microscopy. Consequently, pathways for mitochondrial quality control and cellular clearance were activated, evidenced by the upregulation of PINK-1 (mitophagy), HSP-6 (mitochondrial stress), LGG-1 (autophagy), and the transcription factor HLH-30. Validation experiments using the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC) confirmed this mechanism. While NAC treatment effectively rescued neurodegeneration and motor deficits, it only partially mitigated the molecular damage in the co-exposure group, underscoring the severity of the synergistic interaction. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that Cu and Fe co-exposure induces synergistic neurotoxicity mediated primarily by an oxidative stress-driven autophagy/mitophagy pathway.

title: Comparisons of psychiatric diagnoses, medication prescription patterns, and psychiatric care utilization in first-degree relatives and spouses of individuals with and without Borderline Personality Disorder.
abstract: Small-scale studies have shown that the next-of-kin of individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) face elevated risk of symptoms of mental illness. Little is known about whether these increased symptoms correspond to psychiatric disorders. The aim of this study was to examine the risk of psychiatric disorders, use of psychotropic medication, and utilization of psychiatric care in the next-of-kin of individuals with BPD. Individuals diagnosed with BPD in Sweden, from 2011-01-01 to 2022-12-31, were matched (1:3) by age and sex to individuals without BPD. The study and control cohorts comprised the first-degree relatives and spouses of individuals with BPD and matched controls (n = 24,769 vs n = 77,728). Cox proportional hazards and Poisson regression models assessed associations between having a next-of-kin with BPD and outcome measures during five years post index. After adjustment for potential confounders, the next-of-kin in the BPD cohort exhibited an increased risk of any of the included disorders (HR 2.08; 95% CI 1.94-2.24), as well as higher rates of psychiatric care utilization (IRR 2.21; 95% CI 2.13-2.29), including inpatient care (IRR 2.23; 95% CI 2.02-2.47), and psychotropic medication use (HR 1.75; 95% CI 1.65-1.85), compared with the next-of-kin in the control cohort. In this nationwide study, the next-of-kin of individuals with BPD exhibited increased risk of psychiatric disorders, higher use of psychotropic medication, and greater utilization of psychiatric care. This study highlights the need of adequate care for individuals with BPD and emphasizes the importance of providing support to their next-of-kin.

title: Tear-fluid glial fibrillary acidic protein combined with optic-nerve ultrasonography for non-invasive assessment of cerebral involvement in severe pre-eclampsia: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: To determine whether serum and tear-fluid glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), anti-GFAP autoantibodies, and optic-nerve ultrasonography are associated with disease severity in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and to explore whether their combination adds to the identification of severe pre-eclampsia. This prospective cross-sectional study included 184 pregnant women equally allocated to normotensive pregnancy, gestational hypertension, moderate pre-eclampsia, or severe pre-eclampsia (n = 46/group). Serum GFAP and anti-GFAP autoantibodies were measured in all participants, and tear-fluid GFAP in a predefined subgroup (22/group). Standardized optic-nerve ultrasonography assessed optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD), optic disc height (ODH), optic nerve diameter, and scleral canal diameter. Associations were analysed using non-parametric statistics, Spearman correlation, and receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Between-group differences in biomarkers and ultrasonographic parameters, correlations with disease severity, and discrimination of severe pre-eclampsia by ROC analysis. Serum GFAP increased only in severe pre-eclampsia, whereas tear-fluid GFAP increased progressively from moderate to severe disease (both P < 0.001). Anti-GFAP autoantibodies peaked in moderate pre-eclampsia. Tear-fluid GFAP correlated strongly with ODH (r = 0.772) and with clinical severity (all P < 0.001). ONSD (AUC 0.984) and ODH (AUC 0.973) were the most accurate individual markers; tear-fluid GFAP (AUC 0.908) outperformed serum GFAP (AUC 0.744). Tear-fluid GFAP rises earlier than serum GFAP and tracks ultrasonographic signs of raised intracranial pressure, supporting it as a non-invasive marker of astroglial injury in pre-eclampsia. Optic-nerve ultrasonography provides the strongest discrimination of severe disease. Prospective multicentre studies with neurological outcomes are needed before clinical implementation.

title: Working memory neural correlates after ketamine in treatment-resistant depression: a randomized placebo-controlled functional magnetic resonance imaging study.
abstract: Ketamine exerts rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but its impact on working memory and neural circuitry remains unclear. This secondary analysis investigated behavioral and neural changes during a working memory task post-ketamine infusion in TRD participants versus healthy volunteers (HVs). Data were previously collected from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover trial of 22 unmedicated TRD participants (14F/8 M) and 19 matched HVs (12F/7 M). Participants received ketamine (0.5mg/kg) and placebo two weeks apart. 3T fMRI was acquired during an N-back task at baseline and two days post-ketamine. Accuracy, reaction time, and differential neural activation during 3-back versus 1-back contrasts were analyzed. Ketamine significantly reduced Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale scores compared to placebo (p < 0.01). N-back task performance did not significantly differ between drug conditions. In region of interest (ROI) analyses, TRD participants showed reduced activation in the superior temporal gyrus versus HVs (p < 0.01) after both infusions, and both groups demonstrated decreased parieto-occipital junction activation post-ketamine versus post-placebo (p = 0.01). Baseline dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activity significantly predicted post-infusion activity (p < 0.01). Ketamine's antidepressant effects occurred without significant changes in working memory performance, though region-specific task-related brain changes were observed. Interpretation is limited by modest sample size and the exploratory nature of the ROI analyses. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: www.clinicaltrials.gov, NCT00088699.

title: Early self-regulation in context: Multidimensional organization of neonatal non-nutritive sucking and its association with subclinical maternal depressive traits.
abstract: From the very first days of life, infants' affective regulation unfolds within a dyadic co-regulatory system shaped by caregiver responsivity. In contexts of reduced maternal availability, such as maternal depressive states, infants may be required to compensate for diminished interpersonal regulation by increasingly relying on their internal resources. Neonatal non-nutritive sucking (NNS) represents one of the earliest spontaneously available regulatory behaviors, contributing to physiological and behavioral homeostasis from birth. However, it remains unclear whether its spontaneous organization is associated with early relational vulnerability indexed by maternal depressive symptoms. The present study aimed to characterize the spontaneous organization of NNS in a sample of newborns (N = 42) and to examine whether individual differences in NNS are associated with maternal postnatal depressive subclinical traits measured using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). Results from an exploratory principal component analysis indicated that neonatal sucking behavior was organized along two functional dimensions, reflecting overall sucking effort and behavioral activation, and the temporal organization of sucking bursts. Importantly, higher maternal depressive traits, though subclinical, were selectively associated with increased sucking effort, with infants of mothers reporting higher depressive traits showing more frequent and intense sucking, while no differences emerged for the organizational dimension. Overall, these findings suggest that individual differences in maternal depressive traits within the subclinical range may be associated with neonatal NNS effort, a precocious compensatory mobilization of regulatory resources, potentially serving both to support autonomous regulation and to elicit maternal engagement.

title: Integrated NULISA-based CSF neuroimmune profiling identifies microglial-axonal injury signatures and their clinical and MRI associations in new-onset Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is characterized by inflammatory demyelination, neuroaxonal injury and progressive neurodegeneration. The biological processes driving the disease are already active at clinical onset, yet comprehensive characterization of different molecular pathways at diagnosis remains limited. To integrate high-sensitivity NULISA-based CSF biomarker profiling with neurological impairment at clinical presentation, MRI lesion burden, and microstructural diffusion metrics in normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) in treatment-naïve newly diagnosed MS patients. CSF samples were collected from 70 treatment-naïve newly diagnosed MS patients and 11 age- and sex-matched non-inflammatory neurological controls (NINCs). A CNS Disease Panel of 120 CSF biomarkers was quantified using ultra-sensitive NULISA technology. Differential expression analysis across the NULISA panel was controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR). Secondary multivariable regression and partial-correlation analyses evaluated associations with baseline EDSS, short-term change in EDSS following high-dose corticosteroid treatment, white matter lesion volume, and NAWM ADC measures. These secondary analyses were considered exploratory. Seven biomarkers were significantly increased in MS compared with controls after FDR correction: REST, IL-16, CHI3L1, NfL, ICAM-1, TREM2, and CHIT1. Correlation analysis demonstrated clustering among markers of glial and innate immune activation (CHI3L1, TREM2, CHIT1) and moderate associations between NfL and glial markers. REST was strongly correlated with IL16, suggesting early transcriptional and immune pathway interplay. In multivariable models, higher levels of glial activation markers were associated with neurological impairment at clinical presentation in exploratory multivariable analyses. CSF NfL levels correlated with white matter lesion burden and were significantly associated with diffusion abnormalities in NAWM, particularly in the genu of the corpus callosum, cingulum, and anterior corona radiata, These exploratory associations link CSF NfL with both focal lesion burden and selected NAWM microstructural abnormalities. High-sensitivity NULISA profiling identified co-occurring inflammatory, glial, and neuroaxonal injury signals at MS onset and exploratory associations with clinical and MRI measures, supporting the feasibility of this approach for characterizing early MS biology. NULISA-based CSF profiling captures complementary neuroimmune and neuroaxonal injury signals in treatment-naïve MS at diagnosis. Prospective studies are needed to determine their longitudinal clinical relevance.

title: Interfloor noise triggers sleep fragmentation and affective deficits via dysregulation of the orexin-serotonin axis and hippocampal synaptic plasticity.
abstract: Residential interfloor noise is an urban stressor with unknown neurobiological effects on sleep and mood. This study aimed to elucidate the effects of interfloor noise on sleep architecture, affective behavior, and molecular biomarkers using a mouse model. The post-exposure sleep-wake states of male C57BL/6 mice exposed to simulated interfloor noise (70-100 dB) for 12 h daily for 7 days were monitored via piezoelectric sensing, which was followed by behavioral tests for anxiety- and depression-like phenotypes. Molecular analyses were performed to quantify neuroendocrine, neuroinflammatory, neurotransmitter, and synaptic plasticity markers in the hypothalamus and hippocampus. Exploratory hippocampal RNA-seq was used to assess transcriptomic alterations. Seven days of interfloor noise exposure induced sleep fragmentation (increased bout frequency and shortened duration) and selectively reduced REM sleep while preserving total and NREM sleep. Mice exposed to interfloor noise exhibited anxiety-like behaviors and behavioral despair, and molecularly, they had increased hypothalamic cytokines (tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6, and interleukin-1β) and decreased serum corticosterone. Interfloor noise induced hypothalamic orexin-serotonin dysregulation, increased hippocampal GABAergic signaling, and reduced hippocampal HTR1A, HTR2A, BDNF, PSD95, and p-ERK expression. Hypothalamic markers were correlated with sleep disruption, whereas hippocampal markers were correlated with anxiety. RNA-seq revealed the upregulation of Hif3a and oxygen response transcriptomic changes, indicating an additional hippocampal stress response. The 7-day interfloor noise paradigm provides a valid mouse model for REM sleep disruption, fragmentation, and mood deficits. This study offers a platform for future mechanistic and interventional studies of interfloor noise-induced disorders.

title: Sleep as a vulnerability marker in clinical high-risk populations. a multimodal systematic review.
abstract: Sleep disturbances are increasingly recognized as clinically significant features of the psychosis risk state, yet no comprehensive synthesis has examined sleep across all assessment modalities in clinical high-risk (CHR) populations. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, five major databases were searched (January 1995-March 2026) for original studies assessing sleep in CHR populations, with CHR status operationalized through validated instruments. From 5218 citations, 26 studies were included. Sleep disturbances affected 59-80% of CHR individuals. Actigraphy predicted positive symptom worsening at 12-month follow-up. Experience sampling identified nocturnal awakenings as predictors of next-day paranoia and derealization, mediated by morning negative affect. Sleep disturbance predicted symptom severity over time, accelerated transition among converters, and was independently associated with suicidal ideation. High-density EEG polysomnography documented reduced prefrontal spindle duration, elevated non-rapid eye movement (NREM) gamma power, and reduced slow wave density - replicated across independent cohorts. A multimodal neuroimaging study identified whole-thalamus-dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) hypoconnectivity as a convergent thalamocortical marker. Sleep disturbances in CHR populations span multiple neurobiologically distinct domains. Polysomnographic markers - spindle parameters and NREM gamma power - represent the most neurophysiologically specific signatures identified. Standardized sleep assessment should be integrated into CHR clinical protocols as both a prognostic tool and a modifiable therapeutic target.

title: Myeloid deficiency of the PRC2 complex protein JARID2 promotes foam cell formation through elevated plasma lipids without altering atherosclerosis progression.
authors: van Roomen Cindy P A A
abstract: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease in which macrophages drive plaque development, progression, and eventual destabilization. Epigenetic modulation of macrophages may offer a promising approach to reduce disease progression and residual inflammatory risk that persists despite lipid-lowering therapy. EZH2, the catalytic subunit of PRC2 responsible for depositing H3K27me3, a histone modification associated with gene silencing, is pro-atherogenic in macrophages, while the contribution of PRC2 co-factors remains unexplored. We found the co-factor Jumonji AT-Rich Interactive Domain 2 (JARID2) to be upregulated in unstable human atherosclerotic plaques, prompting us to investigate its role in atherosclerosis. To investigate the role of macrophage Jarid2 in atherosclerosis, we generated myeloid-specific Jarid2-deficient mice (Jarid2del; LysMCreJarid2fl/fl). Bone marrow from Jarid2del or control (Jarid2wt) mice was transplanted to Ldlr-/- recipients, followed by a high cholesterol diet for 9 weeks to induce atherosclerosis. Myeloid Jarid2 deficiency modestly increased plasma cholesterol and triglyceride levels and enhanced foam cell formation. Despite increased plasma lipid levels, atherosclerotic lesion size and composition remained unchanged. Single-cell RNA sequencing of aortic arch plaques revealed that Jarid2 deficiency has both pro- and anti-inflammatory effects in multiple myeloid subsets. Together, the elevated plasma lipid levels and mixed context-dependent inflammatory phenotype suggest that opposing, potentially compensatory mechanisms counterbalance each other, resulting in no net change in overall plaque size. JARID2 is upregulated in unstable human atherosclerotic plaques, whereas myeloid Jarid2 deficiency in mice modestly elevates plasma lipid levels and promotes foam cell formation without affecting atherosclerosis progression.

title: Trends in Antipsychotic Initiation and Use Among Adults With Dementia, 2016-2025: A Pharmacoepidemiologic Study Using the TriNetX Research Network.
journal: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association
abstract: To examine prescribing trends in prevalence and initiation of individual antipsychotics among a predominantly US-based cohort of adults with dementia from 2016 to 2025, with demographic stratification and formal trend analysis. Retrospective cohort study. This study used TriNetX Research Network data from 111 health care organizations. Adults aged ≥65 years with dementia between January 1, 2016 and December 31, 2025 were included; individuals with prior psychotic disorders were excluded. Eighteen Food and Drug Administration-approved antipsychotics, including 14 second-generation and 4 first-generation agents, were identified from electronic health record prescription data. Annual prevalence and initiation (proportion and rates) were calculated overall and by age, sex, and race. Joinpoint regression was used to estimate annual percent change (APC) and average APC in initiation. Among 950,573 patients with dementia (mean age, 82 years; 56.4% female), the prevalence of antipsychotic use increased from 2016 to 2025. Quetiapine and haloperidol were the most frequently used agents, increasing from 3605 to 18,432 and from 4745 to 15,829 per 100,000, respectively. Olanzapine prevalence increased from 1205 to 9264 per 100,000 patients. Initiation rates rose substantially, driven by select antipsychotics; quetiapine initiations increased nearly 5-fold, whereas olanzapine showed a steep increase (average APC, 30.51%; P < .001). Use was highest among individuals aged 75 to 84 years and varied by sex and race. Joinpoint analyses demonstrated late-period acceleration for several agents, including quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone, and brexpiprazole. Antipsychotic use in dementia increased substantially over the past decade, driven primarily by rising initiation of selected agents. These findings highlight marked agent-specific and demographic heterogeneity in prescribing patterns and underscore the need for continued monitoring of antipsychotic use in this high-risk population.

title: Sensorimotor expertise effects extend from dance to face perception.
abstract: Domain specific expertise affects neural and behavioral processes of perception and memory. We explore if sensorimotor expertise extends to other relevant social mechanisms, such as the neural processing of emotional faces. We recorded brain activity of 26 dancers and 26 non-dancers using visual and somatosensory evoked potentials (VEPs, SEPs) during an emotion and sex discrimination task on happy, afraid, and neutral faces. We predicted expertise-related modulation of visual facial emotion processing in visual and somatosensory areas. EEG results revealed distinct visual and somatosensory ERP patterns in the two groups. VEP findings showed that dancers distinguished between neutral and emotional faces at N170 and P200. Non-dancers differentiated between the three emotions with more lateralized processing. For SEPs, dancers uniquely showed early emotion effects (P50) in central somatosensory regions and task-modulated somatosensory engagement at later stages (N80, P100). Non-dancers showed later, localized somatosensory effects. In summary, dance expertise shapes both visual and somatosensory processing of facial emotion, indicating a broader neural representation of emotions. These findings provide novel evidence for a differential facial emotion processing in dancers, extending the dance expertise modulation beyond perception of dance-specific stimuli, to face emotion perception. Overall, this work highlights the strong influence of sensorimotor training on emotion perception.

title: Cell-type specific and nanoscale control of hippocampal presynaptic homeostatic plasticity.
abstract: The lifelong continuity of neuronal function rests upon the perdurance of neurons, synapses and neural circuits that are sustained, in part, by homeostatic signaling. Currently, the implementation of homeostatic signaling within complex brain circuitry remains poorly defined. Given the tremendous diversity of cell and synapse types, is homeostatic plasticity deployed in a cell-type specific manner and, if so, what are the rules? Here, we report that presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) is achieved in a target neuron-specific manner. PHP is robust at synapses that contact parvalbumin-positive (PV+) and absent at somatostatin-positive (SST+) interneurons. Furthermore, PHP can be differentially induced at adjacent synapses that are present within single axonal boutons, separated by hundreds of nanometers. These highly localized effects are eliminated in the absence of Sema3A signaling, a homeostatic signaling molecule. Our data suggest a model where PHP is repressed throughout axons that contact SST+ interneurons and locally de-repressed with nanoscale precision.

title: Neuroprotective Effect of Magnoflorine Through Inhibition of Caspase-3-Mediated Neuronal Apoptosis: In Silico to In Vitro Validation.
journal: Journal of biochemical and molecular toxicology
abstract: Neurodegeneration is a progressive biological phenomenon that is significantly driven by neuronal apoptosis. The current study aimed to investigate the neuroprotective potential of Magnoflorine, a natural alkaloid, by inhibiting Caspase-3-mediated neuronal apoptosis induced by Kainic acid. The caspase-3-inhibiting property of Magnoflorine was initially predicted using in silico methods such as molecular docking, MMGBSA analysis, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, taking Kainic acid as the reference neurotoxic ligand. Molecular docking and MMGBSA analysis showed that Magnoflorine has a higher binding affinity for caspase-3 than that of Kainic acid, which predicts the potential of Magnoflorine to inhibit caspase-3 expression. MD simulations further highlighted this potential through the greater stability of the Caspase-3-Magnoflorine complex than the Caspase-3-Kainic acid complex over 200 ns of simulations. It was finally evaluated through multiple in vitro techniques such as the MTT cell viability assay, LDH cytotoxicity assay, Annexin V-PI apoptosis assay, and immunocytochemistry performed on the retinoic acid-differentiated SH-SY5Y cells. MTT and LDH assays revealed that Magnoflorine significantly improved the viability of differentiated SH-SY5Y cells by reducing Kainic acid-induced cell death and cytotoxicity. The apoptosis assay also showed that Magnoflorine significantly reduced the Kainic acid-induced apoptosis in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells. Inhibition of Caspase-3 by Magnoflorine became evident during immunocytochemistry through the reversal of the Kainic acid-induced increase in Caspase-3 expression in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells, as observed from immunofluorescence intensity. The present study suggests that Magnoflorine is emerging as a valuable therapeutic agent for neurodegeneration by alleviating neuronal apoptosis, which requires further validation through in vivo studies.

title: Psychotropic Drug GST Interactions: In Vitro Inhibition, Molecular Docking, and Translational Potential in Cancer Therapy.
journal: Journal of biochemical and molecular toxicology
abstract: Psychotropic drugs are widely used to treat mental disorders, but they also influence cellular pathways linked to cancer. One key enzyme, Glutathione S-transferase (GST), is involved in detoxification and drug resistance in tumors, making it a potential target in cancer therapy. This study examined the effects of selected psychotropic agents aripiprazole, fluoxetine hydrochloride, risperidone, haloperidol, and sodium valproate on GST activity derived from equine liver. Enzyme kinetics were assessed in vitro using 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene (CDNB) as the substrate and ethacrynic acid (Kᵢ = 4.7 ± 0.8 nM) as the standard reference inhibitor. IC50 values were determined, and inhibition constants (Kᵢ) were calculated via Lineweaver-Burk plot analysis. The ranked Kᵢ values were as follows: Haloperidol (2.80 ± 1.6 nM) < Ethacrynic acid (4.70 ± 0.8 nM) < Risperidone (4.90 ± 0.39 nM) < Fluoxetine hydrochloride (5.40 ± 1.0 nM) < Aripiprazole (6.10 ± 0.7 nM) < Sodium valproate (386.0 ± 0.0 nM). Haloperidol showed the strongest GST inhibition among the tested drugs, even exceeding ethacrynic acid in binding affinity. This suggests its potential as a GST modulator in cancer therapy. Molecular docking studies revealed that the highest binding affinities were observed for Risperidone and Aripiprazole, showing scores of -7.350 to -7.576 Kcal/mol for 9GSS and -8.786 to -8.982 Kcal/mol for 5JCU. These strong interactions indicate a high potential of both compounds to effectively bind within the GST active site. The molecular dynamics simulation confirmed the stability and consistency of these complexes throughout the simulation period. Given the anticancer role of GST inhibitors, psychotropic drugs with significant GST inhibition especially haloperidol may positively contribute to cancer treatment.

title: Age and Neuroimmune Diseases.
abstract: With the aging population accelerating, age has become a core factor influencing the clinical phenotypes, treatment responses, and prognoses of neuroimmune diseases (NDs), including those affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS). This cross-disease review summarizes the shared and specific age-related characteristics of NDs, focusing on the pathological basis of immunosenescence and neurodegeneration underlying age-related ND progression. We extract the clinical manifestations, immune and neural mechanisms of elderly ND patients, and evaluate the challenges and individualized adjustment principles of therapeutic strategies for this population. We explore the age-related immune dysregulation features between NDs and other systemic autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), type 1 diabetes (T1D)). This review aims to construct a cross-disease framework for the precision management of NDs in the aging era, identify research gaps and future directions, and emphasize age-adapted intervention strategies for optimizing the prognosis of elderly ND patients.

title: Antibacterial and pro-osteointegrative bioactive coatings on titanium implant surfaces for oromaxillofacial applications: a systematic review and bayesian network meta-analysis of preclinical studies.
abstract: Numerous preclinical studies have investigated bioactive coatings on titanium implant surfaces to enhance antibacterial and osteointegrative performance in oromaxillofacial applications. However, these studies employ heterogeneous experimental methods and biological outcomes, making it difficult to identify which coating strategies hold the greatest translational potential. This systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA) aimed to rank titanium coating strategies published over the last five years according to their biological performance, using a quantitative statistical framework. Nine coating categories of increasing compositional complexity, ranging from single-component (inorganic, organic, peptides/growth factors) to two-component and three-component formulations combining these classes with each other or with antibiotics, were compared across six biological outcomes in preclinical models. Inclusion criteria followed the PICOS framework for studies published between 2020 and 2025. Three databases were searched according to PRISMA 2020 and its NMA extension. Mean difference (MD) was used for outcomes on a common scale; ratio of means (RoM) when measurement units were heterogeneous. Treatment ranking was estimated using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). Study reporting quality and data completeness were assessed, and studies with insufficient quantitative data were excluded from the quantitative synthesis. Of 143 records identified, 59 met the inclusion criteria and 40 contributed to the quantitative synthesis. SUCRA rankings indicated that three-component hybrid coatings incorporating antibiotics achieved the highest antibacterial performance and osseointegration, while inorganic coatings functionalized with peptides or growth factors demonstrated superior osteogenic differentiation. Organic coatings combined with peptides or growth factors showed the greatest cell proliferation. These findings provide the first evidence-based ranking of bioactive coating strategies for titanium implant surfaces, suggesting a potential advantage of multi-component formulations over single-agent approaches across biological outcomes. The identified compositional complexity gradient may inform the rational design of future multifunctional coatings and help prioritize candidates for further preclinical and translational validation in oromaxillofacial applications.

title: Unleashing the potential of saturation-transfer MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) in neuro-oncology: quantitative molecular CEST and MTC mapping.
abstract: Neuro-oncology biomarkers allow probing tissues beyond anatomical or relaxation contrast. However, new techniques are needed to achieve mechanistic elucidation and effective therapeutic interventions. Quantitative MRI techniques, such as T1, T2, diffusion, and perfusion imaging, provide insights into tumor biology, infiltration, microstructure, and hemodynamics, and have been implemented clinically, but are limited in probing cellular and molecular changes. Saturation transfer (ST) MRI methods, including magnetization transfer contrast (MTC) and chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST), exhibit enhanced sensitivity to semisolid macromolecular content, mobile proteins, tissue metabolites, and acidosis. Despite these advantages, ST-MRI techniques typically have been qualitative or semi-quantitative, time-consuming, and impractical for clinical implementation. However, emerging ST-MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) represents a significant analytical advancement by integrating RF saturation preparation into a pseudo-randomized MRF acquisition framework with a deep learning-based reconstruction. This approach enables simultaneous, clinically realistic, quantitative mapping of bulk water relaxation properties (e.g., T1 and T2), semisolid macromolecular parameters, and exchangeable solute dynamics (e.g., pool size ratios and exchange rates). We provide a comprehensive background, methodological principles, and evolving clinical applications of ST-MRF in neuro-oncology. We explore current advancements, strengths, limitations, and future possibilities for clinical translation into neuro-oncology workflows, including tumor characterization, treatment response monitoring, infiltration mapping, and biomarker development.

title: MORSE-PI: flexible and artefact-free image reconstruction for structural and functional QSM and other phase-critical imaging applications.
abstract: Phase imaging applications such as QSM are highly sensitive to noise amplifications, phase singularities, and other artefacts, particularly in challenging scenarios such as ultra-high field (7 T), under-sampled or single-echo acquisitions. We present a novel image reconstruction method, MORSE-PI, designed to produce high-SNR, artefact-free, and singularity-free phase images for both structural (SWI, QSM) and functional (fQSM) phase-based brain imaging. MORSE-PI extends our previous approach, MORSE, by introducing a Virtual Reference Coil (VRC).
